title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Silence fell over the room. The countess looked at her guests with a pleasant smile, though she made no effort to hide the fact that she wouldn't be upset if they got up and left. The visitor's daughter was already smoothing down her dress and glancing at her mother when suddenly, from the next room, came the sound of boys and girls running toward the door, a chair toppling over, and a thirteen-year-old girl burst in, clutching something hidden in the folds of her short muslin dress, and stopped dead in the middle of the room. She had clearly not meant to run this far. Behind her in the doorway appeared a university student with a crimson collar, a Guards officer, a fifteen-year-old girl, and a plump, rosy-faced boy in a short jacket.
The count leapt to his feet and, swaying side to side, threw his arms wide open around the little girl who had come running in.
"There she is!" he cried, laughing. "My darling, the birthday girl! My sweetheart!"
"My dear, there is a time and place for everything," the countess said with pretended sternness. "You spoil her, Ilya," she added, turning to her husband.
"How do you do, my dear? Happy name day to you," said the visitor. "What a delightful child," she added, turning to the mother.

This black-eyed, wide-mouthed girl — not pretty, but bursting with life — with her childish bare shoulders still heaving from running, her bodice shaking, black curls tossed back, thin bare arms, little legs in lace-trimmed drawers, and feet in low slippers — was at that enchanting age when a girl is no longer a child but not yet a young woman. Breaking free from her father, she ran to bury her flushed face in the lace of her mother's shawl, completely ignoring the stern remark, and began to laugh. Through broken sentences she tried to explain something about a doll she pulled from the folds of her dress.

"Look!... My doll... Mimi... Look..." was all Natasha could manage to say — everything struck her as hilarious. She leaned against her mother and burst into such a loud, ringing fit of laughter that even the prim visitor couldn't help joining in.
"Now then, off you go and take your little monster with you," said the mother, pushing her daughter away with mock severity, and turning to the visitor she added: "She's my youngest."
Natasha raised her face from her mother's shawl for a moment, glanced up through tears of laughter, and buried her face again.
The visitor, forced to witness this family scene, felt obliged to take some part in it.
"Tell me, my dear," she said to Natasha, "is Mimi a relation of yours? A daughter, I suppose?"
Natasha didn't like the visitor's condescending tone toward childish things. She made no reply and just looked at her seriously.

Meanwhile the younger generation — Boris, the officer, Anna Mikhaylovna's son; Nicholas, the university student, the count's eldest son; Sonya, the count's fifteen-year-old niece; and little Petya, his youngest boy — had all settled into the drawing room and were clearly trying to contain the excitement and laughter shining in all their faces within the bounds of good manners. Obviously the conversation in the back rooms, from which they had burst out so eagerly, had been far more entertaining than the drawing room talk of society scandals, weather, and Countess Apraksina. Now and then they glanced at each other, barely able to hold back their laughter.

The two young men, the student and the officer, childhood friends, were the same age and both good-looking, though quite different. Boris was tall and fair, with a calm, handsome face and regular, refined features. Nicholas was shorter, with curly hair and an open expression. Dark hairs were already showing above his lip, and his whole face radiated energy and enthusiasm. Nicholas blushed when he entered the drawing room. He obviously tried to think of something to say but couldn't. Boris, on the other hand, found his footing immediately and began telling — calmly and with humor — how he had known the doll Mimi when she was still quite a young lady, before her nose was broken, how she had aged in the five years he'd known her, and how her head had cracked right across the skull. As he spoke he glanced at Natasha. She turned away from him and looked at her younger brother, who was screwing up his eyes and shaking with suppressed laughter, and, unable to hold herself back any longer, she leapt up and dashed from the room as fast as her nimble little feet could carry her. Boris did not laugh.
"You were about to go out, weren't you, Mama? Shall I have the carriage brought round?" he asked his mother with a smile.
"Yes, yes, go and tell them to get it ready," she replied, returning his smile.
Boris quietly left the room and went to find Natasha. The plump boy ran after them, annoyed that their plans had been disrupted.
